input: In this study, the performance of a copper-zinc oxide catalyst for the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to dimethyl ether is investigated in two different physical forms, namely a structured form and a conventional pellet form. The experiments were carried out at a temperature of 230 °C and a pressure of 60 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition throughout. Performance was evaluated in terms of space-time yield, defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, together with the pressure drop across the catalyst bed and the loss of activity over time. The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of only 0.2 bar, whereas the pellet catalyst delivered a space-time yield of 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 at a considerably higher pressure drop of 1.32 bar. In terms of stability, the activity loss after 100 h on stream amounted to 8% for the structured catalyst, compared with 19% for the pellet catalyst. These results clearly demonstrate that, under the conditions examined, the structured form offers a substantially higher yield while simultaneously imposing a much lower pressure drop, and it also retains its activity more effectively over the duration of the test. It is important to note that both catalysts were evaluated at the single feed composition stated above, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested during this work. Furthermore, it should be pointed out that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge in the literature, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether, and the physical form of the catalyst sets the pressure drop that accompanies a given yield. A structured form and a pellet form of the catalyst are compared at 230 °C and 60 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. Space-time yield, pressure drop, and activity loss were recorded for each form under the conditions stated. Space-time yield (the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour) was 0.93 kg L-1 h-1 for the structured catalyst and 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 for the pellet catalyst. The yield is stated per unit catalyst volume, so the comparison between the forms is made on the volume each charge occupies rather than on its mass. Pressure drop was 0.2 bar for the structured catalyst and 1.32 bar for the pellet catalyst. Activity loss after 100 h was 8% for the structured catalyst and 19% for the pellet catalyst. At the stated conditions the structured form gives the higher yield at the lower pressure drop, and its activity falls more slowly over the test. The two advantages fall to the same form, and no trade-off between yield and pressure drop appears at these conditions: the pellet form's lower yield is not accompanied by a lower pressure drop, and on both measures the pellet form stands behind the structured form. The comparison is limited to the one feed composition tested, at the stated temperature and pressure, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the paired values are stated together here so that the yield comparison and the pressure-drop comparison rest on the same test.
